author: Mikael Häggström
caption: At the shoulder, the rounded top of the upper arm bone (the ball) sits in a shallow cup of the shoulder blade (the socket), so the arm can move in all directions.

author: Mikael Häggström
caption: At the elbow, the end of the upper arm bone fits into a curved notch in a forearm bone like a door hinge, so the arm can only bend and straighten.

author: Ptrump16
caption: The knee is a hinge joint. The gap between the thigh bone and the shin bone looks empty because cartilage does not show up on an X-ray.

author: Louisa Howard
caption: Cilia on the lining of an airway, magnified thousands of times: these tiny hairs sweep mucus, with trapped dust and microorganisms, up towards the throat.

author: Yale Rosen
caption: A slice of lung under a microscope: the white spaces are alveoli, and the pink walls between them are extremely thin, so gases have only a short distance to diffuse.

author: Louisa Howard
caption: Two mitochondria in a cell from a mammal's lung, magnified many thousands of times with an electron microscope. Aerobic respiration happens inside them.

author: Vinayaraj
caption: A germinating seed: its young shoot and root grow fast, so its cells respire quickly and release energy, some of it as heat.

author: Justinc
caption: Lentils are a cheap, healthy source of protein (for growth and repair) and of iron (for making haemoglobin).

author: Mohammed Moussa
caption: A camel in the Egyptian desert: its hump is a store of fat, which the camel uses for energy when food is scarce.

author: Capt. John Yossarian
caption: Magnesium burning in air with a dazzling white flame. The white powder and smoke are magnesium oxide: magnesium + oxygen → magnesium oxide (an exothermic reaction).

author: Metabisulfite
caption: Copper carbonate is a green powder. When it is heated strongly it breaks down into black copper oxide and carbon dioxide — a thermal decomposition.

author: Echinaceapallida
caption: Real blood under a light microscope (stained): many pale red blood cells with no nucleus, and one white blood cell with a large purple nucleus.

author: Electron Microscopy Facility, NCI-Frederick
caption: Electron microscope image with colours added: a red blood cell (red) showing its dimpled, biconcave shape, a white blood cell (blue) and a platelet (yellow).

author: Arthur Jan Fijałkowski
caption: Bunsen burner flames: with the air hole closed you get the yellow safety flame (1); as the air hole is opened the flame turns blue and much hotter (4).

author: Akaniji
caption: Water in a glass tube curves down in the middle (a meniscus). Read the scale with your eye level with the bottom of the curve.

author: Justin Urgitis
caption: Sodium is stored under oil to keep air and water away. Freshly cut faces are shiny, but the dull white surfaces have already reacted with the air (tarnished).

author: Ozone aurora / Philip Evans
caption: Potassium reacting with water: the hydrogen given off burns with a lilac flame. The pink streaks are an indicator in the water showing that alkaline potassium hydroxide is forming.

author: James St. John
caption: A gold nugget from Australia. Gold is so unreactive that it is found in the ground as the shiny metal itself, not combined in an ore.

author: ولاء
caption: Sand dunes in the Great Sand Sea, part of Egypt's Western Desert: a hot desert ecosystem, where very few plants grow and most animals shelter in burrows during the day.

author: Sovernigo
caption: The coral reef at Ras Mohammed in the Red Sea: corals, cracks and caves, sand and the open water above give many different habitats in one ecosystem.

author: Vasuforenv
caption: Water hyacinth forming a thick mat on a river: it blocks the light from the water plants and algae below, and fish can die from lack of oxygen.

author: Alexander Vasenin
caption: A lionfish on a Red Sea reef, where it is a native species. In the Caribbean and western Atlantic it has few predators, so it has become invasive.

author: Tim Denholm
caption: Gold leaf, hammered so thin that it crumples like tissue paper. Gold can be beaten thinner than any other metal, so Geiger and Marsden could use a gold foil only a few hundred atoms thick.

author: Oscar
caption: Black ink after paper chromatography: the solvent has carried its dyes up the paper and separated them into red, green and dark bands, so the ink is a mixture.

author: Pbak4622
caption: Paper chromatography of four inks. The pencil start line is above the water, and each ink separates into different coloured dyes as the water soaks up the paper.
